messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Khalid, a seventy‑five‑year‑old sculptor of Lebanese descent, had spent his life coaxing stone into forms that reflected his quiet reverence for beauty. He lived alone after his wife of fifty years had died a year earlier, and his small studio on the corner of Maple and 5th Street was both his sanctuary and his workshop. On a humid July afternoon, as Khalid climbed a narrow ladder to reach a marble block that weighed close to two hundred and fifty pounds, his hip gave out. The block tumbled down onto the concrete floor, shattering a glass of water and splintering his right arm in a jagged fracture that required a tourniquet and a long hospital stay. The accident left him with a permanent limitation in his arm’s range of motion, chronic pain that pulsed with every small movement, and a scar that reminded him daily of the day his body betrayed him. In the weeks after the accident, Khalid’s mind began to fill with questions and fears. He sat in the quiet of his studio, staring at the fractured hand on a wooden stool, and asked himself, “Why me? Why did this happen to me?” These thoughts were not mere curiosity; they were the beginning of a belief that his body was unreliable, that the injury had permanently changed him for the worse, and that his body had been damaged beyond repair. The sense of physical vulnerability settled like a heavy stone in his chest. When he felt a sharp pang in his wrist while lifting a small tool, he would pause and wonder if the pain was a sign of a new injury, a reminder that his body was now a threat to itself. The weight of the marble block that he once wielded with ease now seemed a challenge too great for his compromised limb. Because he had come to believe that his body could not be trusted and that it was permanently damaged, Khalid began to search for meaning in the accident. He spent hours at his workbench, poring over old photographs of his late wife and the finished sculptures she had adored, trying to find a lesson in the tragedy. He started to monitor his body with a precision that bordered on compulsive, checking his arm for any sign of swelling or tingling, and avoiding any situation that could stress his body further. When the wind carried the scent of rain through his open studio window, he would feel a tremor in his chest and instinctively retreat to a corner where he could watch the rain without moving his arm. In the days that followed, he refused to leave the studio after dark, fearing that the dim light would make him trip and cause another injury. The negative appraisal of his own physical limitations became the lens through which he viewed every movement. He stopped sculpting large blocks and instead turned to smaller, less demanding projects—tiny figurines carved from softer clay. Yet the sense of loss was palpable. Khalid had always felt that sculpting was his way of speaking to the world, and the new restriction cut into his sense of identity. He began to feel that his artistic voice was silenced, that the world around him was moving on while he was trapped in a body that no longer allowed him to create freely. The fear that he might never again produce the works that had brought him joy gnawed at him each time he approached a blank slab of marble. For months, Khalid’s days blurred together in a routine of careful movements, repeated self‑checks, and solitary work on small pieces. His isolation grew as he declined invitations from local art guilds, convinced that any social interaction would require physical exertion he could no longer perform. The studio, once alive with the hum of tools, now felt more like a cage. He would sometimes cry silently at night, the pain in his arm a constant reminder of the day he had lost the trust in his own body. When Khalid finally called the therapist’s office, it was after a night in which the fear of the next tremor in his wrist paralyzed him. He realized that his avoidance of the studio was not just a physical protection; it was also a refusal to face the grief of a lost identity. He was most afraid that he would never again stand in front of the gallery that had displayed his work, that the community would forget the artist behind the stone. Yet beneath that fear was a fragile hope: that he could regain a sense of safety, that his body might be trusted again, and that he could reclaim his place at the workshop, even if it meant adapting his craft rather than abandoning it entirely.
